article_title: Dual Language Programs
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2023, December). Dual language programs. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Three-component implementation pattern for dual language programs
description: Table 2 of the report describes three components of dual language program implementation: program leadership and support (a school leadership team of teachers and administrative staff overseeing model selection, development, and evaluation, with district or state training and funding); hiring and training linguistically and culturally competent teachers in both languages; and aligned curriculum, assessments, and instruction in both languages, including a scope and sequence aligned across subjects and grades in both languages.
requirements: Schools establish a school leadership team consisting of teachers and administrative staff responsible for selecting, advocating for, and overseeing the program model.

Teachers must be trained on how students develop bilingualism and biliteracy and, especially for two-way programs, learn how to incorporate student cultural and linguistic backgrounds into instruction.
Schools develop or adopt a scope and sequence and ensure alignment of the curriculum across subjects and grades in both languages.
constraints: Neither study provides specific information about the implementation of the school leadership team, and one study does not provide information on how the schools were supported.
target_learners: elementary and middle school students in one-way and two-way dual language programs
target_learning_goals: bilingualism and biliteracy
academic language development across content areas
examples: In one study the state developed a curriculum aligned with the Common Core standards designed to promote literacy in both languages, plus lesson plans and translated content curricula for math, social sciences, and science.
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2023, December). Dual language programs. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/726

article_title: Schools Can't Do It Alone: Envisioning a Statewide System of Support to Advance School-Based Behavioral Health in California
citation: Eisenberg, L., Krausen, K., & Caparas, R. (2024). Schools can't do it alone: Envisioning a statewide system of support to advance school-based behavioral health in California. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Any statewide behavioral health TA model should combine cross-agency collaboration with a dual focus on student outcomes and sustainable service infrastructure
description: Research for this project suggests design features for capacity-building TA in school-based behavioral health. First, collaboration across county agencies (COEs, county behavioral health, SELPAs) is critical so services are coordinated and funding maximized; the existing AB 2083 cross-agency county-level MOU structure could be leveraged. Second, the brief recommends "the need for capacity-building TA on both of these areas of focus": improving student behavioral health outcomes (e.g., finding meaningful outcome measures) and building infrastructure for sustainable access (e.g., breaking down funding silos, increasing Medi-Cal reimbursements, developing data-sharing MOUs). Third, access should be expanded without making TA a requirement.
requirements: Collaboration between county agencies regardless of which agency leads TA at the county level
constraints: An analogous statewide measure for student behavioral health does not currently exist, so Tier 2 eligibility would have to rely on proxies such as LEA demographics, Dashboard data, or CHKS data
target_learners: Local educational agencies and community-based partners statewide
target_learning_goals: Improving student behavioral health outcomes and building sustainable infrastructure for integrated systems of care
examples: The brief proposes prioritizing Tier 2 access using LEA demographic data, Dashboard data most closely linked to behavioral health, California Healthy Kids Survey data, or a future SEL-related statewide measure.
key_sources: Eisenberg, L., Krausen, K., & Caparas, R. (2024). Schools can't do it alone: Envisioning a statewide system of support to advance school-based behavioral health in California. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655750

article_title: Making Dual Enrollment Work: Solving the Access-Success Paradox with OUSD's Point Person Model
citation: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Roldan-Rueda, D., & Blanchard, A. (2026). Making dual enrollment work: Solving the access–success paradox with OUSD’s point person model. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Invest in professional learning and partnership infrastructure for both college instructors and school-based support staff
description: The report finds the point person model functions because both sides receive training. Before entering the classroom, new instructors attend a course agreement meeting; they then "participate in professional development sessions at least twice per semester on topics that include adolescent brain development, mastery-based grading, and scaffolding strategies." OUSD partners with San Francisco State University to offer courses and stipends for dual enrollment instructors, while point people receive tools, templates, and training with autonomy to adapt to context. This dual investment creates a shared understanding of student needs and instructional strategies.
requirements: A dedicated district coordination team, partnership agreements with the community college, and funding for stipends and professional development
constraints: The report quotes district staff that the model is not very affordable; scaling requires deliberate investment in staffing, professional development, and institutional commitment
target_learners: High school students in dual enrollment courses
target_learning_goals: Effective college-level instruction adapted to high school contexts; consistent support for student success
examples: A 20-year instructor described the professional development as revealing a new level of teaching, and a college dean observed that the district specialist effectively taught one instructor to teach.
key_sources: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Roldan-Rueda, D., & Blanchard, A. (2026). Making dual enrollment work: Solving the access–success paradox with OUSD’s point person model. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED681373

article_title: Perceived AI empowerment and threat in relation to university students' dependence on GenAI: the indirect role of trust in AI
citation: Zhu K, Ma Y, Zhang J and Liu J (2026). Perceived AI empowerment and threat in relation to university students' dependence on GenAI: the indirect role of trust in AI. Front. Psychol. 17:1940317. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1940317
title: Dual-appraisal model of GenAI dependence integrating cognitive appraisal theory and trust theory
description: The article proposes a dual-appraisal model in which perceived AI empowerment and perceived AI threat are two relatively independent cognitive appraisals that shape university students' dependence on GenAI, both directly and indirectly through trust in AI. Drawing on cognitive appraisal theory and trust theory, it treats trust as "an important psychological pathway linking students' appraisals of GenAI with their reported reliance on the technology." Empowerment appraisals are associated with greater trust and dependence, threat appraisals with lower trust and dependence, and the two appraisals coexist rather than forming opposite ends of one continuum.
requirements: Measurement of perceived AI empowerment, perceived AI threat, trust in AI, and AI dependence as distinct validated constructs; the article's scales showed Cronbach's α from 0.933 to 0.954 and discriminant validity via Fornell–Larcker and HTMT criteria.
constraints: The study is cross-sectional, single-source self-report, so the model describes associations rather than causal effects; common method bias cannot be ruled out entirely, and the sample was a convenience sample of Chinese university students.
target_learners: University students with prior GenAI experience
target_learning_goals: Understanding and managing students' reliance on generative AI in academic learning, including maintaining independent judgment and verification when using AI support
examples: In the 360-student survey, the model explained 42.7% of variance in trust in AI and 45.9% of variance in AI dependence, with significant direct and indirect paths in both appraisal pathways.
key_sources: Zhu K, Ma Y, Zhang J and Liu J (2026). Perceived AI empowerment and threat in relation to university students' dependence on GenAI: the indirect role of trust in AI. Front. Psychol. 17:1940317. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1940317

article_title: Preparing Students for AI-Powered Materials Discovery: A Workflow-Aligned Framework for AI Literacy, Equity, and Scientific Judgment
citation: Dongming Mei, Katherine Moore, and Ben Sayler. (2026). Preparing Students for AI-Powered Materials Discovery: A Workflow-Aligned Framework for AI Literacy, Equity, and Scientific Judgment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09624
title: Dual-track AI education: foundational AI courses combined with disciplinary integration
description: The paper recommends a dual-track structure in which stand-alone AI foundations courses teach data preparation, algorithm design, validation, uncertainty, and responsible use, while AI is embedded inside disciplinary courses so students see how assumptions and data quality change by domain. The authors state 'The two tracks should not operate as separate silos,' since foundational courses provide tools and disciplinary integration shows how those tools behave in real knowledge-making environments.
requirements: Foundational and disciplinary tracks must reinforce each other through shared projects, contextual feedback, and evidence from authentic applications
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in science and engineering
K-12 and higher-education students more broadly
target_learning_goals: knowing when to rely on AI, how to verify outputs, and how to maintain human responsibility in high-stakes decisions
examples: Figure 2 depicts foundational AI courses and disciplinary integration jointly producing AI-literate graduates

article_title: AiAWE: An Open-Source LLM Automated Writing Evaluation System Using LoRA-Adapted Instruction-Tuned Models
citation: John Maurice Gayed. (2026). AiAWE: An Open-Source LLM Automated Writing Evaluation System Using LoRA-Adapted Instruction-Tuned Models. A PREPRINT. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12801
title: Dual-purpose LoRA adaptation: adapter carries scoring, preserved base model carries feedback generation
description: The article proposes that LoRA adaptation on an instruction-tuned checkpoint can yield one model serving two purposes: because LoRA freezes base weights and learns only a small low-rank update, "the original model’s general-purpose instruction-following and text-generation capabilities are largely preserved during adaptation." The adapter was trained on score-only targets (the bare human score, no feedback), yet at inference the fine-tuned model "produces well-formed feedback despite never having been trained on feedback examples." The authors attribute the scoring behavior to the adapter and the feedback formatting to the preserved instruction-following of the base model. Keeping adapters unmerged at inference is described as a deployment convenience, not a determinant of the dual-purpose behavior.
requirements: Fine-tuning via LoRA (weights frozen, low-rank adapter only) on an instruction-tuned checkpoint, rather than full fine-tuning, so base generative capabilities survive adaptation
constraints: The capacity-preserving effect weakens as rank grows; at higher ranks the adapter can overwrite instruction-following behavior needed for structured output, as observed for LLaMA above rank 64
target_learners: Adult L2 English learners
University writing students
target_learning_goals: Numeric essay scoring against a rubric
Rubric-referenced qualitative writing feedback
examples: The production prompt requests a JSON object with both a score and a structured reasoning field, and the score-only-trained model produces the reasoning field
key_sources: John Maurice Gayed. (2026). AiAWE: An Open-Source LLM Automated Writing Evaluation System Using LoRA-Adapted Instruction-Tuned Models. A PREPRINT. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12801

article_title: Bayesian Consensus Calibration of Continuously Evolving IRT Item Banks
citation: Paul A. Jewsbury and Steven W. Nydick and Manqian Liao and Siyuan (Marco) Chen. (2026). Bayesian Consensus Calibration of Continuously Evolving IRT Item Banks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13590v1
title: Duolingo English Test operational calibration data used for the empirical evaluation
description: The evaluation applied consensus calibration to operational response data from the Duolingo English Test, described as "a high-volume, continuously evolving language assessment" measuring two latent dimensions with items in several response formats (selected-response, partial-credit, and continuous). Each period was calibrated by a scalable Bayesian explanatory IRT engine with period-specific item posteriors thinned to approximately 1,000 draws. The run comprised four consecutive quarterly calibration periods spanning approximately one year with the third period defining the reference metric.
requirements: A scalable Bayesian explanatory IRT calibration engine per period
Consecutive calibration periods with a designated reference period
constraints: Each period included on the order of tens of thousands of items and hundreds of thousands of examinees
The benchmark was fit with a separate ability distribution per period (a multiple-group model) to match the ability structure of the per-period calibrations
target_learners: Duolingo English Test examinees
target_learning_goals: language-proficiency scoring and adaptive item selection in a high-stakes assessment
examples: Linking used the robust per-draw criterion solved for 200 draws of each non-reference period; the consensus Gaussian was sampled to provide 2,000 draws per item
key_sources: Paul A. Jewsbury and Steven W. Nydick and Manqian Liao and Siyuan (Marco) Chen. (2026). Bayesian Consensus Calibration of Continuously Evolving IRT Item Banks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13590

article_title: AI-Powered Math Tutoring: Platform for Personalized and Adaptive Education
citation: Jarosław A. Chudziak and Adam Kostka. (2025). AI-Powered Math Tutoring: Platform for Personalized and Adaptive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12484
title: Dual-memory personalization framework (long-term memory and working memory)
description: The platform personalizes tutoring through a dual-memory framework: long-term memory (LTM) stores persistent, student-specific data such as prior knowledge, misconceptions, learning preferences, and goals, while working memory (WM) maintains the context of the current learning session, including topic, problem state, and recent interactions. These modules inform the Tutor Agent and content generation components, enabling proactive support such as targeted hints when a known misconception like difficulty with negative sign distribution occurs, or function plotting for students who prefer visual explanations.
requirements: A Memory Dispatcher to oversee conversations and control the appropriate memory modules
constraints: Current personalization operates on a basic set of attributes, per the authors' stated limitation
target_learners: mathematics students with varying prior knowledge and learning paces
target_learning_goals: individualized tutoring responsive to student misconceptions and preferences
examples: If LTM knows a student usually has difficulty understanding negative sign distribution, the system proactively offers targeted hints or corrective feedback

article_title: Demystify, Use, Reflect, Assess (DURA): An Experience Report on LLM Integration in CS2
citation: Margaret Ellis, Nikitha Donekal Chandrashekar, Sehrish Basir Nizamani, Mohammed Farghally, Jake O'Brien, and Naren Ramakrishnan. (2026). Demystify, Use, Reflect, Assess (DURA): An Experience Report on LLM Integration in CS2. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30908
title: DURA (Demystify-Use-Reflect-Assess): a lightweight framework for incorporating LLMs into courses
description: DURA is the article's four-component framework for updating courses to incorporate AI/LLMs: Demystify how LLMs work and how they affect learning; Use LLMs with guidance and attribution; Reflect on LLM use and problem-solving; and Assess programming assignment skills through proctored assessments with retakes. The authors call it "our lightweight framework for incorporating LLMs into courses" and apply it in a large flipped CS2 course of 442 students. They state its components "deliberately support the learning process, as well as the need for reliable evidence of student learning," with demystification as the foundational component.
requirements: The assess component is course specific and time-intensive, requiring question banks to support retakes, which the authors note was not reliable to generate without oversight
Supporting test review and retakes requires support by the instructional team
constraints: The authors position the changes as manageable initial steps before overhauling labs and projects, and cannot attribute outcomes causally due to lack of a control group
target_learners: undergraduate CS2 (data structures) students
instructors adapting CS courses for LLM use
target_learning_goals: meeting course learning outcomes without LLM assistance
effective and ethical LLM use
metacognition and self-regulation around LLM use
examples: In CS2: a 30-minute week-2 LLM demystification lesson, attribution statements on every code file, reflection assignments in weeks 4, 8, and 13, and reallocation of 20% of the course grade to proctored assessments with retake days one week after each test

article_title: When universities advocate GAI but practice falls short: student appraisals and creative process engagement in art education
citation: Chen Y (2026) When universities advocate GAI but practice falls short: student appraisals and creative process engagement in art education. Front. Psychol. 17:1955192. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1955192
title: Dual-path cognitive appraisal model of GAI advocacy–practice inconsistency
description: The article proposes a dual-path model grounded in the transactional theory of stress and coping, in which perceived GAI advocacy–practice inconsistency is appraised simultaneously as a hindrance and as a challenge, each carrying an opposing indirect association with creative process engagement. As the article states, "we propose a dual-path model in which GAI advocacy–practice inconsistency is associated with students' creative process engagement through hindrance and challenge appraisals." Pathways thinking is incorporated as a boundary condition that differentially shapes the two indirect relationships. The model extends organizational word–deed alignment research to GAI-supported art education.
requirements: Students must perceive a discrepancy between institutional GAI commitments and actual implementation for the appraisal process to operate
constraints: The scenario manipulation captured a broader experience of inconsistent implementation rather than an isolated word–deed inconsistency effect
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate art students in higher education
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement in creative processes such as problem identification, information searching and encoding, and idea generation in GAI-assisted art learning
examples: Study 2 tested the full model with PLS-SEM on 425 students' actual GAI-supported art-learning experiences, including direct, indirect, moderating, and conditional indirect relationships.

article_title: From Enhancement to Over-Reliance: A Mixed-Method Study of Generative AI and Sustainable Learning Performance
citation: Gao L, Sun Y and Khan SU (2026) From enhancement to over-reliance: a mixed-method study of generative AI and sustainable learning performance. Front. Psychol. 17:1847369. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1847369
title: Dual-pathway model of generative AI use and sustainable learning
description: The article integrates three theories — AI literacy, self-regulated learning, and cognitive offloading — into a dual-pathway model in which effective AI use opens both a positive path to sustainable learning performance and a negative path through AI over-reliance. The authors state that "the same behaviors that constitute eﬀective AI use can, under conditions of reduced self-regulation or elevated polychronicity, activate the over-reliance pathway". Polychronicity moderates both pathways as an individual-difference variable. The model is positioned against technology-acceptance approaches that measure intention to use rather than learning outcomes.
requirements: Students must actually engage with generative AI tools in academic work for the pathways to be observed
Measurement of AI literacy, SRL, critical AI evaluation, effective AI use, over-reliance, polychronicity, and sustainable learning performance as distinct constructs
constraints: Developed and tested in Chinese higher education with purposively sampled AI-using students
Sustainable learning performance is measured as perceived, self-reported retention, independence, and transfer
target_learners: university students using generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: sustainable knowledge retention
independent application of learning
transfer of understanding across contexts
examples: The model was tested with PLS-SEM on a three-wave time-lagged survey of 623 Chinese university students and elaborated with 15 educator interviews

article_title: From information providers to learning designers: heutagogical teaching practices in AI-enhanced education
citation: Hochberg N and Waitzman R (2026). From information providers to learning designers: heutagogical teaching practices in AI-enhanced education. Front. Educ. 11:1905833. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1905833
title: Dual-layer relationship: teacher reflective regulation and critical AI literacy mediate learner-facing agency and capability design
description: The article proposes a dual-layer, developmental process in which teacher-level self-regulated reflection and critical AI literacy preserve professional judgment when working with generative systems, and that judgment is then enacted in learning designs intended to support learner agency and capability. The authors write that "At the teacher layer, self-regulated reflection and critical AI literacy help preserve professional judgment in interaction with probabilistic systems." AI-supported design connects the layers but does not guarantee learner self-determination.
requirements: Teachers' developing self-regulation, reflective practice, and design autonomy; explicit testing in future classroom research
constraints: The dual-layer relationship remains a proposition for future testing rather than a demonstrated student outcome
target_learners: in-service teachers participating in AI-focused professional development
target_learning_goals: designing learning environments that support learner self-determination and capability
examples: The article links the proposition to Arvatz et al.'s (2025) finding of parallel progression in teachers' self-regulated learning and students' reflective capacities, while keeping the learner-outcome claim explicitly untested

article_title: Ethical implications of prompt injection in AI-mediated grading: An adversarial red-team evaluation
citation: Niklas Humble. (2026). Ethical Implications of Prompt Injection in AI-mediated Grading: An Adversarial Red-Team Evaluation. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09758-9
title: Dual role of prompt engineering techniques and contextual vulnerability in AI-mediated academic work
description: The article contributes a domain-specific account in which the same prompt engineering techniques promoted for output quality — "iterative refinement, personification, and the use of example templates" — are also highly effective when repurposed for prompt injection attacks, differing primarily in intent. It extends prompt injection research into situated academic work practices such as grading, showing how documented techniques can interact with a real institutional AI tool in ways that override safeguards, and emphasizes contextual vulnerability of AI-mediated assessment for fairness, integrity, and trustworthiness.
requirements: An AI tool used for academic work that processes attached external content such as student submissions
constraints: Derived from a single AI tool, one grading scenario, and a controlled set of prompt injection techniques; academic trust was not empirically measured
target_learners: higher education faculty
higher education students
target_learning_goals: understanding how AI tools process prompts and can be manipulated
security-aware AI use in academic work
examples: The red-team evaluation applied instruction manipulation, role-playing, obfuscation, and payload splitting against Copilot grading a synthetic failing essay across five attempts

article_title: K-12 in-service teachers' beliefs about generative AI in classrooms: insights from the United States, India, Qatar, Colombia, and the Philippines
citation: Xiu RL, Aguilar SJ, Macías AJ, Shikanova A, Al-Sulaiti R, Junjunia M and Jebril ST (2026) K-12 in-service teachers’ beliefs about generative AI in classrooms: insights from the United States, India, Qatar, Colombia, and the Philippines. Front. Educ. 11:1929017. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1929017
title: Dual-lens framework: SDT explains positive GenAI beliefs while Attribution Theory explains GenAI concerns
description: The article integrates Self-Determination Theory and Attribution Theory into a "dual-lens framework" in which SDT accounts for the motivational conditions (autonomy, competence, relatedness) underlying positive beliefs, while Attribution Theory interprets how causal attributions about plagiarism and creativity sustain concern. Survey constructs are mapped onto SDT needs as approximate proxies: institutional support for relatedness, comfort with technology for competence, and perceived usefulness for autonomous motivation. The framework generates competing predictions about whether readiness lowers or preserves concern, which the cross-national design tests.
requirements: Survey constructs must be mappable onto SDT's three psychological needs, which the authors note are measured only via proxies rather than directly
constraints: The authors state the SDT mappings are approximate and need satisfaction is not measured directly; cross-sectional data preclude causal inference
target_learners: K-12 in-service teachers
target_learning_goals: Formation of beliefs and concerns about generative AI in teaching and learning
examples: The study mapped institutional support to relatedness, comfort with educational technology and English proficiency to competence, and perceived usefulness to autonomous motivation in a five-country survey

article_title: LLM-Based Educational Simulation: Evaluating Temporal Student Persona Stability Across ADHD Profiles
citation: Jana Gonnermann-Müller, Jennifer Haase, Nicolas Leins, Thomas Kosch, Sebastian Pokutta. (2026). LLM-Based Educational Simulation: Evaluating Temporal Student Persona Stability Across ADHD-Related Persona Specifications. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06307
title: Dual-assessment framework for evaluating LLM human simulations via joint self-report and observer-rated persona measurement
description: A methodology adapted from clinical psychology that jointly measures self-reported characteristics and observer-rated behavioral expressions of an LLM persona. Self-report scores measure how the persona agent characterizes itself when directly prompted with questionnaire items, while observer-report scores measure which persona-relevant behaviors are expressed in generated narratives or conversational segments. The framework's central contribution is exposing self–observer dissociation: "LLMs reliably report the assigned persona when directly asked, yet their spontaneous behavioral expression of that persona degrades in unscripted conversation." It also distinguishes between-conversation from within-conversation stability as complementary temporal dimensions.
requirements: Requires a validated instrument with parallel self-report and observer-report forms (here the CAARS ADHD Index) and independent raters blind to persona instructions
constraints: Neither measure provides direct access to the model's internal state; the framework measures consistency of expression, not representational validity or clinical authenticity
target_learners: LLM-simulated students with ADHD-related persona specifications
target_learning_goals: Temporal stability of simulated learner personas across and within interactions
examples: Experiment I administered the 26-item CAARS self-report short form to persona agents and had three independent LLM raters complete the 30-item observer short form on each narrative

article_title: Navigating AI in STEM: What Secondary Students Actually Do With Generative AI-Driven Tools
citation: Martin Lnenicka and Petr Coufal. (2026). Navigating AI in STEM: what secondary students actually do with generative AI-driven tools. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00637-8
title: Dual AI literacy as interdependent operational and epistemic workflow phases, with cognitive mediation mapped as substitution versus verification
description: The article proposes that effective generative AI use requires "a fundamental duality of literacy: operational AI literacy (prompting, iterative refinement) and epistemic AI literacy (verification, methodological evaluation, bias awareness)". These dimensions are treated not as orthogonal psychometric traits but as overlapping, interdependent behavioral phases within a unified problem-solving workflow. The study operationalizes cognitive mediation behaviorally by mapping self-reported workflows into categories of substitution (cognitive offloading) versus verification (active comparison of logic), and its qualitative findings indicate prompting loops heavily overshadow external factual validation.
requirements: Both operational prompting competence and epistemic verification competence must be cultivated within the same task workflow for responsible AI use
constraints: The framework is descriptive and behavioral, not an evaluation of latent psychometric traits; individual epistemic beliefs were not directly measured
target_learners: secondary students in STEM subjects
target_learning_goals: AI literacy
epistemic verification of AI outputs
independent reasoning in STEM problem solving
examples: The survey coded behavioral interaction configurations into three functional roles: substitution (replacing reasoning), supplementation (extending reasoning), and verification (checking reasoning)

article_title: From One-Size Texts to Tailored Readings: Student Experiences with AI-Generated Course Materials
citation: Sidorkin, A. M. (2026). From One-Size Texts to Tailored Readings: Student Experiences with AI-Generated Course Materials. Open Praxis, 18(3), 506–522. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.3.1141
title: Dual tailoring: simultaneous individualization of readings along interest and comprehension-level dimensions within an AI-mediated workflow
description: Dual tailoring is the article's descriptive design label (explicitly "not a new theory") for an instructional configuration combining two individualization dimensions in one AI-mediated workflow. Interest tailoring adapts readings to professional context, sector, and role through examples and cases; comprehension-level tailoring adjusts "pacing, scaffolding, explanatory depth" via definitions, stepwise structures, and check-for-understanding prompts. Both are supported by iterative prompting, in which students request follow-ups to reframe, deepen, simplify, localize, or apply a first-pass reading.
requirements: Requires iterative prompting: students must request follow-up questions rather than accept a single generated text, with instructor-controlled constraints through the reading prompt template.

citation: Fu Jinbin & Zhao Fang. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081393
title: Dual connectedness framework: mental health impacts depend on AI connectedness paired with traditional connectedness
description: The article's core interpretive model holds that 'the mental health impacts of artificial intelligence connectedness depend on its relative level paired with traditional offline connectedness rather than its absolute intensity alone.' When traditional bonds satisfy adolescents' identity confirmation demands, AI connectedness acts as a supplementary protective factor; when human caregivers fail to recognize real inner demands, it produces compensatory substitution effects. The framework integrates competing viewpoints such as displacement versus stimulation hypotheses into a single system and is claimed to explain conditional shifts that single constructs like AI attachment cannot.
requirements: Testing the framework requires simultaneously measuring both traditional and artificial intelligence connectedness.
constraints: The framework's propositions are theoretically deduced hypotheses whose validity awaits verification by subsequent empirical research.

citation: Adam M. Lavecchia, Heidi Liu, and Philip Oreopoulos. (2014). Behavioral Economics of Education: Progress and Possibilities. NBER Working Paper No. 20609. http://www.nber.org/papers/w20609
title: Dual-system framework of four behavioral barriers to treating education as an investment
description: The review organizes the behavioral economics of education around a dual-system model of intertemporal choice, in which a forward-looking system and an automatic system weigh current costs against distant benefits. title: Dual-process theory with an added inhibition system as a framework for inhibitory control in learning
description: The review presents dual-process theory as a prominent framework bridging research traditions: System 1 encompasses fast, automatic, intuitive processes, while System 2 involves slower, deliberate, effortful processes. Building on this, Houdé and colleagues proposed a third system, the inhibition system: "This system enables individuals to suppress intuitive or dominant responses, facilitating the shift to the more controlled reasoning associated with System 2." In this framework, inhibitory control is the key mechanism allowing learners to move from heuristic to algorithmic reasoning, applied to both Piagetian tasks and school subjects.
requirements: Learners must suppress automatically activated automatisms before analytical (System 2) reasoning can operate
constraints: Alternative interpretations related to conflict processing or strategy adjustment cannot be entirely ruled out for negative priming effects
target_learners: primary school students aged 6–12
secondary students and adults reasoning about earlier-grade topics
target_learning_goals: overriding intuitive responses in favor of analytical reasoning across school subjects
examples: Explains persistent errors on classical Piagetian tasks in children and persistent errors in adults on primary school topics

article_title: Relationships Between Experiences of Autonomy and Well(Ill)-Being for K-12 Youth: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Amanda Vite, Erika A. Patall, Man Chen. (2024). Relationships Between Experiences of Autonomy and Well(Ill)-Being for K-12 Youth: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review (2024) 36:127. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09967-x
title: Dual process model of basic psychological need satisfaction and frustration
description: The dual process model treats need satisfaction and need frustration as distinct psychological processes rather than opposite ends of one continuum. As the article states, "The dual process model defines need satisfaction and need frustration as distinct processes, with experiences of need satisfaction primarily leading to more optimal outcomes and experiences of need frustration primarily leading to non-optimal outcomes." The meta-analysis used it to predict that matched-valence correlations (ANS with well-being, ANF with ill-being) would be stronger than mismatched ones, a pattern the results supported.
requirements: Studies must measure need satisfaction and need frustration separately to test the model's distinct-process prediction
constraints: The article notes low need satisfaction differs from need frustration: frustration can provoke negative outcomes whereas low satisfaction may only elicit decreased positive outcomes
target_learners: K-12 youth (Kindergarten to 12th grade students)
target_learning_goals: Understanding autonomy need satisfaction and frustration as mechanisms of youth psychological well- and ill-being
examples: The meta-analysis tested and found stronger pooled correlations for matched-valence pairs (ANS-well-being r = .37; ANF-ill-being r = .34) than mismatched pairs

article_title: The Effect of Playback Speed and Distractions on the Comprehension of Audio and Audio-Visual Materials
citation: Ashley Chen, Suchita E. Kumar, Rhea Varkhedi, Dillon H. Murphy. (2024). The Effect of Playback Speed and Distractions on the Comprehension of Audio and Audio-Visual Materials. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09917-7
title: Dual-channel cognitive load account of speeded multimedia comprehension
description: The article explains preserved comprehension at accelerated speeds via cognitive load theory and the multimedia principle: because visual and verbal information are processed in separate working memory channels, adding visual content to narration divides processing demands and frees capacity. The authors state that "multimedia presentations can help mitigate the negative costs of accelerated speeds, especially when information is processed by separate working memory components (i.e., narration in the auditory channel, text or pictures in the visual channel), which reduces cognitive load." This account frames why audio-only content is more vulnerable to overload at high speeds and why visual supports buffer accelerated narration.
requirements: Learning materials must pair narration with visual content (text or pictures) presented in the visual channel so processing is split across channels
constraints: The account is offered as the authors' interpretation of why speed effects were absent up to 2.5x; performance is expected to decline beyond the 2x threshold per prior work the article cites
target_learners: undergraduate students learning from pre-recorded audio and audio-visual lectures
target_learning_goals: comprehension of narrated instructional content at accelerated playback speeds
examples: Experiment 2 compared audio-only versus audio-visual clips (slides plus instructor images) at 1x and 2x speed; Experiment 3 compared textual versus pictorial slides accompanying narration

title: Dual-process model of content generation during writing
description: The article proposes a dual-process model in which two processes generate content during writing. The first is "an active, knowledge-constituting process in which content is synthesized by constraints within semantic memory representing the implicit structure of the writer's understanding". The second is "a reflective, knowledge-transforming process in which content retrieved from episodic memory is manipulated in working memory to satisfy rhetorical goals". The article outlines how these processes are combined and relates them to current models of writing.
requirements: Both processes must operate for effective writing, since "both processes are required for effective writing".

citation: Stephen R. Earl, Ian M. Taylor, Carla Meijen and Louis Passfield (2016). description: Drawing on basic psychological needs theory, the article proposes two separate maladaptive processes: perceived teacher psychological control frustrates autonomy, which directly manifests as energetic, disruptive active disengagement; and frustrates competence, which reduces subjective vitality and thereby produces passive withdrawal such as daydreaming. The authors state the study will "identify different mechanisms underpinning two separate types of pupil disengagement". citation: Van de Sande, E., Kleemans, T., Verhoeven, L., & Segers, E. (2019). The linguistic nature of children's scientific reasoning. Learning and Instruction, 62, 20-26. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.02.002
title: Dual-route (spatial and verbal) framework of individual differences in children's scientific reasoning
description: The article frames scientific reasoning as drawing on parallel visuospatial and linguistic processing, aligned with Baddeley's working-memory model: "there is both a spatial and verbal route to retrieve and restore information from long-term memory", with an episodic route enabling their interaction. Visuospatial inferencing serves pattern discovery in evidence and graphs, while academic vocabulary and linguistic inferencing serve conceptualising, mental-model construction and syllogistic deduction. The study tested this framework by relating both ability types to the full cycle of scientific reasoning skills in sixth graders.
requirements: Assessment of both visuospatial (e.g., Raven's matrices) and linguistic (reading comprehension, academic vocabulary) abilities alongside scientific reasoning measures
constraints: Framework tested only in a cross-sectional design with paper-and-pencil measures at the end of primary school

article_title: A dual-process model for cognitive training
citation: Julia Ericson and Torkel Klingberg. (2023). A dual-process model for cognitive training. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00161-2
title: Dual-process piecewise linear model of cognitive training dynamics
description: A quantitative model describing cognitive training as two simultaneous processes: a fast task-specific improvement and a slow, linear capacity improvement that transfers to untrained tasks. The learning trajectory is a piecewise linear function with two phases — phase 1 includes both task-specific and capacity improvement, phase 2 only capacity improvement — fitted to individual daily performance data via a hidden Markov model whose hidden state is the current phase, with parameters optimized by expectation maximization. The article states "training is not only task speci ﬁc or transferable but a combination of the two" and that the models "provide methods for quantifying and separating these processes".
requirements: Daily performance data from the trained task across the training period, plus repeated transfer test sessions to validate the capacity factor
Individual-level (not group-averaged) training curves, since the task-specific phase is identified only at the individual level
constraints: The transition day was constrained by CFA results to be at most day 10, which affected 4.5% of the population
A longer training period could potentially yield more than two phases
The model assumes the probability of returning from phase 2 to phase 1 is zero and that phase 1 is always the starting phase
target_learners: Children ages 9 to 11 undergoing adaptive working memory training
target_learning_goals: Working memory capacity and transfer to visuospatial, verbal working memory, and arithmetic tasks
examples: Fitted to daily Grid performance of each of the 1300 children, with the median transition day at 3.05 and parameters optimized by expectation maximization

article_title: Offline consolidation mechanisms of the retrieval practice effect: an analysis based on EEG signal characteristics
citation: Jing Zhang, Xiaoning Huo, Hongbo Lv, Jiahua Xu & Xiaofeng Ma. (2025). Offline consolidation mechanisms of the retrieval practice effect: an analysis based on EEG signal characteristics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00349-8
title: Dual-phase consolidation model of retrieval-practiced memories
description: The authors propose a model in which "memory strengthwithin this dichotomous framework develops progressively through ofﬂine processes." Under feedback-free retrieval practice, successfully retrieved items are encoded only once and form conceptually-related semantic memory networks that during sleep "are repeatedly reactivated and replayed, gradually enhancing memory strength." Conversely, restudy tasks do not trigger replay because no relevant semantic networks form during online learning, and feedback-based retrieval does not require offline reprocessing because it "achieve[s] immediate pathway correction via online monitoring mechanisms." The model aligns with the Complementary Learning Systems framework, positing that sleep enhances memory stability through post-retrieval integration and consolidation of semantic networks.
requirements: Requires an offline sleep period following encoding for the no-feedback consolidation pathway to operate
Applies to weakly encoded, feedback-free retrieval-practice memories rather than strongly encoded traces
constraints: The correlational electrophysiological evidence precludes definitive causal inferences about the role of slow wave-spindle coupling in memory
The proposed mechanism is framed within a dichotomous strength framework and rests on nap rather than full-night sleep data
target_learners: Undergraduate learners memorizing paired associative materials
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention of weakly associated verbal material
examples: The nap-vs-wake experiment assigned participants across restudy, retrieval practice with feedback, and retrieval practice without feedback conditions with 90-minute and 24-hour tests

citation: Chengyan Yang, Tongran Liu, Mengxin Wen & Xun Liu. (2025). The distinct functions of working memory and intelligence in model-based and model-free reinforcement learning. npj Science of Learning 10:72. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00363-w
title: Dual-system reinforcement learning framework: model-based versus model-free strategies
description: The article adopts the dual-system RL framework in which "the model-based strategy is characterized by its ﬂexibility and is typically driven by speciﬁc goals, taking current states into account", while "the model-free strategy is more efﬁcient and resource-conserving" and driven by habits and immediate rewards. A validated computational model estimates parameters — learning rate, eligibility trace, inverse temperature, and a mixing weight — that quantify each learner's reliance on the two systems in a two-stage task. The article uses this framework to show that WM load arbitrates between the strategies.
requirements: Estimation requires trial-level behavioral data (choices and obtained rewards) plus the task's environmental transition structure and available options.
constraints: The article notes the relationship between model-based strategy adoption and intelligence is unstable and affected by characteristics inherent in different two-stage paradigms.
target_learners: adult learners in experimental RL tasks
target_learning_goals: understanding how learners arbitrate between flexible planning and habitual responding during feedback-based learning
examples: In the study, a model-based agent who chose the pink door and received nine strawberries from the white bear would subsequently also choose the cyan door leading to that bear, whereas model-free agents relied exclusively on rewards.

citation: Fang Wang, Elizabeth Y. Toomarian, Radhika S. Gosavi, Blair Kaneshiro, Anthony M. Norcia & Bruce D. McCandliss. (2025). title: Contrasting Dual-Route and computational multi-grain-size accounts of the negative brain-behavior correlation in new vocabulary learning
description: The article presents two theoretical frameworks that interpret the negative correlation between learning-sprint SSVEP amplitudes and decoding skill. From a Dual-Route perspective, the pattern reflects "a race between a lexical route and a sublexical decoding route", where weaker decoders show larger learning effects as practice strengthens the lexical route. A computational alternative posits no distinct lexical versus sublexical mechanisms, applying the same learning principles across multiple grain sizes, so less skilled readers rely on larger grain-size mappings that accentuate learned-versus-novel differences. The authors note the data cannot distinguish the frameworks but that they generate testable predictions.
requirements: Future studies contrasting well-formed versus poorly formed nonword strings, or learned versus novel words at various grain sizes such as rime units, to distinguish the two accounts
constraints: The current data cannot directly distinguish the contrasting frameworks, as the article states

target_learning_goals: visual word recognition and vocabulary learning
examples: The article derives that a Dual-Route reading implies no comparable oddball effect for well-formed versus poorly formed nonword strings, whereas the computational framework predicts oddball effects for learned versus novel words at various grain sizes

citation: Chanjuan Fu, Xiaoxin Hao, Xinyue Shi, Hanxin Qian, Shanyun He & Fengji Geng. (2025). Effect of cognitive control strategies on young children’s attention and emotion during coding learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00360-z
title: Dual-mechanism framework of cognitive control integrated with Zimmerman's cyclical phase model of self-regulated learning

Early coding/computational skills

article_title: Semantic relatedness and the efficacy of retrieval practice
citation: Gupta, M.W., Pan, S.C., & Rickard, T.C. (2026). Semantic relatedness and the efficacy of retrieval practice. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00416-8
title: Dual-memory model of test-enhanced learning
description: The dual-memory framework holds that restudy strengthens the retrieval route formed during initial study (study memory), whereas "a test with feedback trial both strengthens study memory and forms a separate memory of the test event (test memory), yielding two independent retrieval routes for the tested items on the final test." A parameter-free quantitative instantiation predicts test-condition accuracy from restudy accuracy (PCT-predicted = 2*PCR − PCR²), with predicted TE = PCR − PCR². Cued-recall training design with one test trial per item for the parameter-free predictions
constraints: The three simplifying assumptions (identical study-memory distributions, identical study and test memory distributions, stochastic independence) are made "on the basis of simplicity and we do not necessarily expect them to hold in the general case"
The model does not anticipate the absent testing effect reported for non-linguistic materials with apparent zero relatedness

target_learning_goals: Long-term retention and recall of paired verbal materials
examples: Rickard and Pan (2018) demonstrated close model fits to mean PCT across 512 participants from multiple cued-recall experiments; Rickard (2020) showed the predictions hold for cumulative proportion-correct distributions

title: D-UDA: a digital didactic learning unit combining an escape room with multisensory games for fifth-grade mathematics
description: D-UDA (unità didattica di apprendimento digitale) is a website-based digital learning unit for fifth-grade mathematics, offered during the first Italian COVID-19 lockdown. The article states that "The D-UDA experience was divided into two parts: the virtual classroom and the virtual archeological site." Transversal competencies such as cooperation and engagement

article_title: Simulation research and design: a dual-level framework for multi-project research programs
citation: Fink, M. C., Radkowitsch, A., Bauer, E., Sailer, M., Kiesewetter, J., Schmidmaier, R., Siebeck, M., Fischer, F., & Fischer, M. R. (2020). Simulation research and design: a dual-level framework for multi-project research programs. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09876-0
title: A dual-level framework describes simulation research and design programs as a research committee plus subordinate projects moving through four phases
description: The article proposes a framework describing a research program as "a dual-level, multi-project system consisting of one research committee and two or more research projects". It passes through four program/project phases: creating a foundation, constructing and adapting simulations and research materials, conducting empirical investigations, and analyzing data and communicating results. Members take on consultant, researcher, designer, and content expert roles, and phases can overlap and iterate. The framework was derived from theory on multi-team systems, Sonnenwald's program stages, and the multi-center simulation research model, and is illustrated with the COSIMA program.
requirements: Applies to research programs with a research committee and multiple subordinate research projects focusing on the assessment and facilitation of knowledge and competences
constraints: Scope limited to programs developing simulations as complex scientific artifacts; phases may overlap and iterate rather than run strictly linearly
target_learners: higher education students in medical and teacher education (the program's research populations)
target_learning_goals: diagnostic competences facilitated through simulation-based learning
examples: The COSIMA program: a research committee of twelve professors coordinating eight projects, seven empirical and one meta-analysis, investigating scaffolding in simulation-based learning environments

article_title: Dual empowerment in VR-based technical training: longitudinal evidence of developmental dynamics in learning outcomes and skill transfer
citation: Min Jou, Yungwei Hao. (2026). Dual empowerment in VR-based technical training: longitudinal evidence of developmental dynamics in learning outcomes and skill transfer. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10654-7
title: Dual Empowerment (DE) framework: staged instructional integration of VR-based cognitive precision and authentic physical practice
description: Dual Empowerment is a developmental instructional design framework in which "Dual Empowerment (DE) refers to the deliberate instructional integration of VR-based simulation and authentic physical practice to support both learning outcomes (LO) and skill transfer/retention (STR)". VR empowerment supplies data-driven feedback, scenario simulation, and safe trial-and-error for precision-oriented learning; physical empowerment reintroduces authenticity, sensory calibration, and practical application under ecological constraints. DE treats the two modalities as interdependent empowerment pathways whose structured, staged coordination—not immersion alone—supports durable competence, extending experience-centered immersive learning models such as CAMIL toward a design model for blended vocational training.
requirements: Both modalities must be structurally coupled rather than loosely connected; the design assumes neither modality alone is sufficient and competence is stabilized only when simulation-informed strategies withstand authentic constraints
constraints: The framework targets skill-intensive vocational domains; the article notes existing frameworks like TPACK, CoI, and Activity Theory do not fully specify how immersive and physical modalities should be coupled over time, which DE addresses
target_learners: vocational education and training (VET) learners in skill-intensive technical domains
target_learning_goals: procedural skill acquisition, durable skill transfer and retention in welding and comparable technical trades
examples: A five-stage welding program operationalized DE with 216 learners, combining real-time performance feedback, visualized learning traces, and structured VR–hands-on transitions
key_sources: Min Jou, Yungwei Hao. (2026). Dual empowerment in VR-based technical training: longitudinal evidence of developmental dynamics in learning outcomes and skill transfer. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10654-7

article_title: Creative intention and persistence in educational robotic
citation: Anaïs Leroy, Margarida Romero. (2022). Creative intention and persistence in educational robotic. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10128-6
title: Dual-process model of the creative process with two inhibitory-control stages
description: The article proposes a model of the creative process based on dual process models, in which achieving a creative solution requires two stages of inhibitory control: first inhibiting the conservative intention to reuse an already known solution, then persisting in the inhibition of familiar associations while searching for a new solution. As the article states, "Being creative is an effortful choice which requires a regulatory process from the creative intention to the creative solution." The study's results are interpreted as coherent with this model, with inhibitory control possibly influencing both creative intention and creative behavior persistence.
requirements: The model presupposes a prior successful solution exists that can be repeated conservatively, as in a repeated task
constraints: The article states the model should also be engaged on other creative tasks to observe if the results apply beyond the educational robotic task
target_learners: adults performing creative problem-solving tasks
target_learning_goals: sustaining creative behavior in repeated problem-solving tasks
examples: In the CreaCube study, conservative intention relied on the fast system building on prior knowledge, while creative intention required inhibiting fixation on the newly learned solution.

article_title: Improving hybrid brainstorming outcomes with computer-supported scaffolds: Prompts and cognitive group awareness
citation: Farrokhnia, M., Noroozi, O., Baggen, Y., Biemans, H., & Weinberger, A. (2024). Improving hybrid brainstorming outcomes with computer-supported scaffolds: Prompts and cognitive group awareness. Computers & Education 227 (2025) 105229. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105229
title: Dual pathways to creativity model (DPCM)
description: The DPCM, proposed by Nijstad et al. (2010), is the explanatory framework this study uses to design and interpret brainstorming scaffolds. It "identifies two cognitive pathways for generating high-quality ideas: persistence and flexibility". Persistence involves deep, systematic exploration within a few idea categories, while flexibility involves exploring broad cognitive categories. The article adapts CSCL scaffolds to target each pathway: SCAMPER prompts for persistence and cognitive group awareness for flexibility, and notes support may strongly stimulate one pathway while weakly or negatively affecting the other.
requirements: Specific process constraints or support such as rules, task structures, and instructions to foster mental engagement in the pathways
constraints: Support mechanisms may strongly stimulate one pathway while weakly or even negatively affecting the other, requiring careful design
target_learners: higher education students performing creative idea-generation tasks
target_learning_goals: generating high-quality, original ideas in individual and group brainstorming
examples: The study operationalized persistence as comprehensible ideas divided by flexibility score, and flexibility as the number of UN Sustainable Development Goal categories covered by a participant's ideas

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of Teachers' Provision of Structure in the Classroom and Students' Academic Competence Beliefs, Engagement, and Achievement
citation: Patall, E. A., Yates, N., Lee, J., Chen, S., Bhat, P., Lee, K., Beretvas, S. N., Guan, S., Cohen, M., Zhai, F., Brecht-Heitz, S., DeLorenzo, D., & Gonzales, K. (2023). A meta-analysis of teachers’ provision of structure in the classroom and students’ academic competence beliefs, engagement, and achievement. Educational Psychologist.
title: Dual process model of engagement within self-determination theory
description: The article draws on the dual process model within a self-determination theory framework, which asserts a differentiated view of teacher practice, student motivation, and student engagement. According to the model, "supportive practices like structure are theorized to be most strongly linked with desirable outcomes, including higher competence beliefs and engagement, rather than undesirable outcomes like disengagement", while thwarting practices that define chaos are expected to be most predictive of undesirable outcomes. Structure supports the psychological need for competence—the need to experience efficacy in one's behavior—whose satisfaction is theorized as necessary for optimizing motivation and learning.
requirements: Teacher practice must remain supportive rather than controlling for the model's predicted benefits to emerge
constraints: The article does not examine chaos or thwarting practices in this synthesis, so the model's predictions about chaos are not tested here
target_learners: Preschool through high school students
target_learning_goals: Academic engagement, disengagement, competence beliefs, and achievement

article_title: Preparing Students for Class: A Clinical Trial Testing the Efficacy between Multimedia Pre-Lectures and Textbooks in an Economics Course
citation: Jose J. Vazquez & Eric P. Chiang. (2016). Preparing Students For Class: A Clinical Trial Testing The Efficacy Between Multimedia Pre-lectures And Textbooks in an Economics Course. Journal of College Teaching & Learning, 13(2). https://clutejournals.com
title: Dual coding theory and the pictorial superiority effect as the cognitive rationale for visual pre-lectures
description: The article grounds its case for multimedia pre-lectures in two research areas: neuroscience of vision and memory, and cognitive science. It invokes dual coding theory, which "suggests that people receive and process information through two distinct but interrelated channels: a verbal channel... and a visual channel". It also cites the pictorial superiority effect, arguing that "the more visual the input becomes, the more likely it is to be recognized and recalled". These accounts imply that adding images to verbal messages enhances retention and that text-only messages risk overloading the verbal channel.
requirements: Presentation must combine verbal and visual channels rather than narrating written words, which the article says may overload the verbal channel
constraints: The article presents this as a summary of prior research (Vazquez and Chiang, 2014), not as a test conducted in this study
target_learners: students with no prior exposure to college or AP-level economics
target_learning_goals: comprehension and retention of introductory economics concepts
examples: The clinical trial's video condition presented dynamic animations synchronized with audio narration, operationalizing dual-channel presentation

article_title: Teaching Vocabulary with Graphic Novels
citation: Ahmet Başal, Talat Aytan & İbrahim Demir. (2016). Teaching Vocabulary with Graphic Novels. English Language Teaching, 9(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n9p95
title: Dual coding / multimedia learning account of combining words and pictures in language materials
description: The article grounds its material design in Paivio's Dual Coding Theory and Mayer's multimedia learning principle, which hold that "People learn more deeply from words and graphics than from words alone" because verbal and visual subsystems jointly encode matched input. It applies this account to justify presenting figurative idioms as text plus illustrations in a graphic-novel storyline, arguing that matched images strengthen memory beyond verbal input alone.
requirements: Materials must present words and pictures that match, so both the verbal and non-verbal systems encode the input
constraints: The article notes that merely using illustrations may not produce achievement gains; how illustrations relate to the text matters
target_learners: foreign language learners at upper-intermediate level
target_learning_goals: learning figurative idioms
vocabulary knowledge in English as a foreign language
examples: The experimental material embedded 40 MICASE figurative idioms in a script converted to a graphic novel with computer software

article_title: The Effect of Learner-Generated Illustrations on the Immediate and Delayed Recall of English Idioms
citation: Afrouz Aeineh, Saeed Moeeni, Hamideh Merati. (2014). The Effect of Learner-generated Illustrations on the Immediate And Delayed Recall of English Idioms. Advances in Language and Literary Studies. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.3p.28
title: Dual Coding Theory: verbal and nonverbal (imagery) subsystems as the basis for learner-generated illustrations
description: The article draws on Paivio's Dual Coding Theory, which posits "two separate subsystems", one specialized for the verbal aspect of language and the other for the nonverbal (imagery) aspect, giving "the same amount of importance to both verbal and nonverbal processing". These systems have internal representations activated when the learner realizes, manipulates and considers a word in mind. The study uses DCT to motivate having learners draw their own mental images of idioms alongside verbal definitions and examples.
requirements: Instruction must engage both the verbal and the nonverbal (imagery) processing subsystems
target_learners: Iranian EFL learners at intermediate proficiency
target_learning_goals: recall of English idioms
examples: The experimental group drew their own mental image of each idiom on paper after verbal clarification, operationalizing dual verbal-plus-imagery coding.

article_title: Effect of Programmed Instruction on Students' Attitude towards Structure of the Atom and the Periodic Table among Kenyan Secondary Schools
citation: M. J. Wangila, W. Martin, M. Ronald. (2015). Effect of Programmed Instruction on Students' Attitude Towards Structure of the Atom and the Periodic Table among Kenyan Secondary Schools. Science Education International, Vol. 25, Issue 4, 488-500. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Science+Education+International
title: Dual Coding Theory as the theoretical basis for combining PI software with conventional instruction
description: The study is based on the Dual Coding Theory of information processing, which has roots in constructivism and postulates that learning is best achieved when information is processed both in the form of images and in the form of words. The theory holds that human cognition consists of two subsystems processing knowledge simultaneously: a verbal subsystem that processes and stores linguistic information and a visual subsystem that processes and stores images and pictorial information; though independently activatable, their interrelations allow dual coding of information. In this study, the conventional approaches used by control groups provided the linguistic forms of SAPT concepts while the PI software provided the imagery forms, hence dual coding for the experimental groups.
requirements: Both verbal and visual representations of the content must be available to learners for dual coding to occur, as when PI is used alongside conventional approaches
constraints: Applied in this study specifically to the abstract Chemistry topic SAPT among form two students
target_learners: form two Kenyan secondary school Chemistry students
target_learning_goals: understanding and positive attitude towards abstract Chemistry concepts (structure of the atom and the periodic table)
examples: The experimental groups received PI alongside conventional approaches, providing imagery and linguistic forms of SAPT concepts respectively

article_title: Humorous Videos and Idiom Achievement: Some Pedagogical Considerations for EFL Learners
citation: Malihe Neissari, Hamid Ashraf & Mohammad Reza Ghorbani. (2017). Humorous Videos and Idiom Achievement: Some Pedagogical Considerations for EFL Learners. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 5(3), 109-127. http://ijltr.urmia.ac.ir
title: Dual coding theory and multiple intelligences as the explanatory framework for video-based idiom instruction
description: The article interprets its findings through two frameworks: Paivio's dual coding theory, which "maintains that application of still or animated pictures can indeed lead to better memory performance due to the association of both visual and verbal information," and Gardner's multiple intelligences theory, which emphasizes integrating multiple intelligences in instructional methods to reactivate hidden potential in learners. The study framed its video-clip intervention as integrating some of these intelligences in instructional and humorous video clips.
requirements: Instruction should integrate visual and verbal information channels, per the dual coding account the article applies.
constraints: The frameworks are used as post hoc interpretation of the study's results, not as directly tested components.
target_learners: Iranian undergraduate EFL learners
target_learning_goals: English idiom learning and achievement
examples: The experimental treatment showed each video clip twice, asked learners to infer idiom meanings from context, and had them use idioms in new sentences with classmates.

article_title: The Effect of Picture Story Books on Students' Reading Comprehension
citation: Roslina. (2017). The Effect of Picture Story Books on Students’ Reading Comprehension. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 8(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.8n.2p.213
title: Dual coding framework for picture story books in reading
description: The article organizes its account of why picture story books help reading around Paivio's dual coding theory, adapted through Mayer's framework into a reading-specific model. Pictures and words present "referential connection in the students' mind", so that as students' eyes move "back and forth between the pictures and the text then students form a comprehension". The verbal system stores the text and the imagery system stores the pictures, and their additive activation is held to facilitate comprehension, word recognition and inference-making.
requirements: Reading material must present pictures together with the accompanying text so both verbal and imagery codes are activated
constraints: The article notes visual and verbal representation are not the only influence; timer frequency of the material also matters
target_learners: low-proficiency EFL readers, including non-formal education students
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension, word recognition, making inferences and organizing information
examples: The researcher drew a logical framework (Figure 5) in which students look at pictures and read words, moving between them to form comprehension, illustrated by student interview comments about predicting text content from pictures

article_title: Improving English Language Learners' Idiomatic Competence: Does Mode of Teaching Play a Role?
citation: Zainab Abolfazli Khonbi & Karim Sadeghi. (2017). Improving English Language Learners’ Idiomatic Competence: Does Mode of Teaching Play a Role? Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research 5(3), 61-79. http://ijltr.urmia.ac.ir
title: Dual coding / mental imagery account of idiom learning from visual and enacted contexts
description: The authors interpret their findings through Paivio’s (1986) dual coding theory, under which a mental image of a concrete scene is formed alongside the verbal form and stored in memory, providing a better tool for learning idioms. They argue this mental image is called up in role-plays and then in movies, explaining why those groups outperformed sentence-use and definition groups. As they put it, the image 'is called up in role-plays and then in movies', providing 'a better condition for both comprehension and retention of new words in general and idioms in particular'.
requirements: Idioms must be presented with visual illustration or enacted scenarios alongside their verbal form for the image-plus-verbal encoding to occur.
constraints: This is the authors' interpretation of their results, attributed to Paivio (1986) and Boers, Eyckmans, & Stengers (2007), not a separately tested mechanism in the study.
target_learners: upper-intermediate/advanced EFL learners
target_learning_goals: comprehension and retention of English idioms
examples: The Movie Group watched YouTube clips illustrating idioms and guessed meanings before the correct meaning and a Persian equivalent were revealed; the Role-play Group performed conversations containing the idioms.

article_title: Effects of Etymological Elaboration on the EFL Learners' Comprehension and Retention of Idioms
citation: Bagheri, M. S., & Fazel, I. (2010). Effects of Etymological Elaboration on the EFL Learners’ Comprehension and Retention of Idioms. Journal of Pan-Pacific Association of Applied Linguistics, 14(1), 45-55. https://www.paaljapan.org
title: Dual Coding Theory as the explanatory account of etymological elaboration's mnemonic effect
description: The article invokes Dual Coding Theory (Clark and Paivio, 1991) to explain why etymological elaboration aids comprehension and retention. On this account, etymological information evokes imagery that is stored together with the verbal form, giving recall a second route: the etymological information "is likely to call up a mental image of a concrete scene" which "can subsequently provide an extra pathway for recall". The article presents this as a plausible explanation, not a tested mechanism.
requirements: The etymological information must be concrete enough to call up a mental image of a scene alongside the verbal form of the idiom.
constraints: The article states the mechanism is not established: "How etymological elaboration helps learners comprehend and retain idioms is not clear yet."
target_learners: Advanced EFL learners (intermediate to advanced, IELTS 5–6)
target_learning_goals: Comprehension and long-term retention of idioms
examples: The study's matching task asked learners to pair 15 idioms with their origins, the treatment the theory is offered to explain.

article_title: The Effect of a Metacognition-Based Instructional Practice on the Metacognitive Awareness of the Prospective Teachers
citation: Burcu Duman, Çetin Semerci. (2019). The Effect of a Metacognition-based Instructional Practice on the Metacognitive Awareness of the Prospective Teachers. Universal Journal of Educational Research 7(3): 720-728. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2019.070311
title: Metacognitive Awareness Scale (MAS)
description: The Metacognitive Awareness Scale is a 31-item, 5-point Likert-type instrument developed by Duman, used to measure prospective teachers' metacognitive awareness across seven sub-dimensions. The article reports "KMO (Kaiser -Mayer-Olkin) value of the scale has been measured as 0,893" and a total reliability coefficient of 0,89, with factor reliabilities ranging from 0,54 (motivation) to 0,80 (evaluation). It served as the sole outcome measure in the pre-test–post-test control group experiment.
requirements: Administered as pre-test and post-test to experimental and control groups to detect change in metacognitive awareness
constraints: The motivation factor's Cronbach Alpha of 0,54 is low, and data were not normally distributed, requiring non-parametric tests
target_learners: prospective teachers in teacher education
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness including planning, awareness, control, regulation, questioning, motivation and evaluation
examples: Applied before and after a 10-week metacognition-based instructional practice in a Testing and Evaluation in Education course

article_title: The Role of Comic Reading Materials in Enhancing the Ability to Read in EFL
citation: Roozafzai, Z. S. (2012). The Role of Comic Reading Materials in Enhancing the Ability to Read in EFL. Journal of English Language Teaching. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ
title: Dual Coding Theory explains how visuals support reading comprehension
description: Dual Coding Theory (DCT) concerns the nature of language and imagery, proposing that "the verbal and visual systems can be activated independently, but there are interconnections between the two systems that allow dual coding the information and cuing from one system to the other." The article uses DCT to explain why comic materials with pictures may enhance reading comprehension: activating both verbal and non-verbal mental representations helps readers create interconnected contexts for generating inferences and integrating texts.
requirements: Reading materials must include visuals that are semantically consistent with the text so both verbal and imagery systems are activated
constraints: The article notes that in L2 contexts it is not clear which type of visual organizers help which kind of learners
target_learners: EFL learners
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension

article_title: A Small Scale Experimental Study: Using Animations to Learn Vocabulary
citation: Kayaoğlu, M. N., Dağ Akbaş, R., & Öztürk, Z. (2011). A Small Scale Experimental Study: Using Animations to Learn Vocabulary. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(2). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Dual-coding theory as the rationale for animation-based vocabulary learning
description: The article grounds its use of animation in dual-coding theory, which holds that "processing language knowledge in both verbal and visual channels make learning effective" (attributed to Pavio). Animation operationalizes this by presenting moving scenes with utterances learners both hear and see simultaneously, engaging multiple senses and supporting autonomous learning. The article uses this account to explain why animation may aid retention and motivation in vocabulary learning.
requirements: Animation content must present the target words' meaning, pronunciation and written form together so both channels are engaged.
constraints: The article notes animations can distract learners into re-watching the cartoon and can hinder learners with vision difficulties if used repeatedly (citing Devi).
target_learners: foreign language learners, including pre-intermediate university EFL students
target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning and retention in a foreign language
examples: The water-cycle animation displayed each phase as moving scenes while students heard and saw the utterances simultaneously, mirroring the dual-channel presentation dual-coding theory describes.
